v.q: You run mvn package. Which phases does Maven execute?
o: Every phase of the default lifecycle up to and including package
Only the package phase and nothing before it
Every phase up to package, then install and deploy as well
Only the phases whose plugins changed since the last build
v.w: Asking for a phase runs all earlier phases in order: compile, test, then package. install and deploy come after package and are not run.

v.q: Which phase runs before package in the default lifecycle?
o: test
install
deploy
clean
v.w: The default lifecycle runs validate, compile, test, package, verify, install and deploy in order. clean is a separate lifecycle.

v.q: What is the difference between a Maven phase and a goal?
o: A goal is a plugin task, and goals are bound to phases to do the work
A phase is a plugin task, and goals are the stages of the lifecycle
Phases run in parallel, whereas goals always run one after another
A goal is a phase that has been renamed in the parent pom
v.w: Phases are named steps with no behaviour. Plugin goals such as compiler:compile are attached to them, and a goal can also be run directly.

v.q: Which statement about Maven goals and phases is NOT true?
o: A phase does the work and a goal only names it
Goals belong to plugins
Phases are bound to goals
You can run a goal directly with mvn plugin:goal
v.w: Goals are the tasks that do the work. A phase is a named stage that goals are bound to.

v.q: Two libraries need different versions of Jackson. Which version does Maven use by default?
o: The one nearest to your project in the dependency tree
The highest version number found anywhere in the tree
The lowest version number found anywhere in the tree
Neither, and the build fails with a version conflict
v.w: Maven uses nearest definition, and the first declared on a tie. It is not the newest, so an older version can win. Manage the version to be sure.

v.q: Your pom declares jackson 2.15 directly, and a library needs 2.12. Which does Maven use?
o: 2.15, the nearest declaration
2.12, the lowest version
Both versions together
Neither, the build fails
v.w: Nearest wins, and a direct declaration is always the nearest.

o: Sets the version and scope to use when an artifact is needed, adding nothing itself
Adds every listed library to the classpath of the project
Removes the transitive dependencies of the listed libraries
Downloads the listed libraries ahead of the next build
v.w: It only declares versions. A dependency still has to be listed in dependencies, but it can then omit the version. A BOM is a pom made of this section.

v.q: Which statement about dependencyManagement is NOT true?
o: It adds the library to every module
It centralises versions
A child module still lists the dependency
It can import a BOM
v.w: It only sets versions and scopes. A module must still declare the dependency to use it.

v.q: Which scope suits a JDBC driver that the code never compiles against?
o: runtime, because it is needed to run but not to compile
provided, because the application server always supplies it
test, because only the integration tests connect to it
compile, because every library must be on the compile classpath
v.w: runtime puts the driver on the runtime and test classpaths but not the compile classpath, and it is packaged with the application.

v.q: Which scope fits a servlet API that the application server provides?
o: provided
runtime
test
compile
v.w: provided means needed to compile but supplied at run time by the container, so it is not packaged.

v.q: In a multi-module build, what decides the order in which modules are built?
o: The dependencies between the modules, worked out by the reactor
The order the modules are listed in the parent pom
The alphabetical order of the module directory names
The size of each module, with the smallest built first
v.w: The reactor sorts modules by their inter-module dependencies, whatever the list order. Circular dependencies cause an error.

v.q: Which option builds only the module app and the modules it depends on?
o: mvn -pl app -am package
mvn -T 4 package
mvn -o package
mvn -q package
v.w: The -pl flag selects a module and -am adds the modules it needs.

v.q: What does mvn install do that mvn package does not?
o: Copies the artifact into the local repository in ~/.m2
Uploads the artifact to the company Nexus server
Runs the integration tests that package skips
Deletes the target directory before it builds
v.w: install is the phase after verify. It copies the jar into ~/.m2 so other local projects can use it. Uploading to a remote repository is deploy.

v.q: Which command copies the artifact to ~/.m2 so other local projects can use it?
o: mvn install
mvn package
mvn compile
mvn verify
v.w: package stops in target. install also puts the artifact in the local repository.

v.q: Why would you use the Maven Wrapper (mvnw)?
o: Everyone and the CI server run the same Maven version without installing it
It makes the compiler faster by keeping the JVM running between builds
It lets a project be built without a pom.xml file
It replaces the local repository with a shared cache
v.w: The wrapper downloads the Maven version recorded in .mvn/wrapper, which removes differences between machines.

v.q: Which file records the Maven version that the wrapper downloads?
o: maven-wrapper.properties
pom.xml in the root
settings.xml in ~/.m2
mvnw.cmd in the root
v.w: The properties file holds the distribution URL. Commit it so every machine uses the same version.
